items.title: Knowing where it is means not knowing where it's going
items.claim: Take an electron and pin down its position to within a hydrogen atom (10 to the minus 10 m). The uncertainty in its momentum is then at least 1.05 times 10 to the minus 24 kg m/s — giving the electron an undetermined velocity of about 11 million metres per second.
items.prompt: Is this 'just' a limitation of our instruments?

options.text: Yes — better lasers will eventually let us measure both exactly
No — it's a fundamental property of conjugate variables in quantum mechanics, baked into the maths (the operators don't commute) regardless of what apparatus you use
Yes — quantum mechanics is approximate and will be replaced
No — measuring position physically kicks the particle, so the uncertainty is a disturbance effect

items.reveal:
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: delta x times delta p is at least h-bar over 2. This is NOT a statement about measurement disturbance, despite the famous 'gamma-ray microscope' thought experiment.

It is a mathematical consequence of position and momentum being represented as non-commuting operators. A state with definite position is a superposition of all possible momenta. A state with definite momentum (a plane wave) is spread over all positions. You cannot have both simultaneously — the states with both definite simply do not exist.

This is why electrons in atoms don't fall into the nucleus. Confining them to the nuclear volume would require enormous momentum uncertainty — and hence enormous kinetic energy. The ground-state size of the hydrogen atom is set by the balance.
items.why: Uncertainty is taught as if it were a measurement problem. It's a structural feature of how nature is built.

items.title: Repeating a measurement reduces one kind of error but not another
items.claim: Measure a length with a ruler 10 times and average — the result is more reliable than any single measurement. Measure with an uncalibrated ruler 10,000 times and the average is still wrong.
items.prompt: Why does averaging help with random error but not systematic error?

options.text: Random errors fluctuate around the true value and partially cancel when averaged (uncertainty falls as 1/√N). Systematic errors shift every measurement in the same direction by the same amount — averaging does nothing
Systematic errors are smaller than random errors

items.reveal:
Random error: unpredictable fluctuations around the true value. Sources: meniscus reading, parallax, sensor noise, vibration. Averaging N independent measurements reduces the standard error by a factor of √N.

Systematic error: every measurement shifted by the same amount in the same direction. Sources: uncalibrated instrument, zero offset, observer bias, faulty technique. Averaging doesn't help.

Good practice: repeat measurements to reduce random error, then calibrate against a known standard to detect systematic error. Report both. Modern lab work distinguishes 'repeatability' (one operator, one instrument, same day) from 'reproducibility' (different operators, different instruments, different days) — they catch different sources of error.
items.why: Students take averages without thinking about which errors averaging can and cannot fix. Real precision needs different techniques for different error types.
